title: Scher Enterprises, Inc. v. Bronco Wine Company
lead: A wine supplier refused to let a distributor transfer its business to a company carrying competing brands and spirits. Conflicting evidence about those policies prevented summary judgment for the supplier.

actors.name: Scher Enterprises, formerly Viviano Wine Importers

proceedings: District court received supplemental evidence on supplier qualifications.
December 11, 2001 order denied Bronco’s summary-judgment motion.
limits: $1.65 million was alleged reduced sale price, not damages; price difference unclear. No final statutory liability or separate pending-delivery claim disposition.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A distributor agrees to sell its business
paragraphs: Viviano Wine Importers distributed several Bronco Wine Company brands in Michigan. J. Lewis Cooper Company signed a purchase letter of intent July 26, 2000, then an asset agreement September 29, amended October 5 for an October 17 closing. Its supplier schedule was absent from the court record; the judge presumed it identified Bronco.

Viviano and Cooper met Bronco’s chief financial officer Fred Franzia in California October 12. Viviano said he voiced no concerns and that it delivered written notice and an approval request October 16. Bronco refused October 25, citing inadequate notice and Cooper’s Gallo distribution. It said a national policy avoided its largest competitors’ distributors when alternatives existed and protected Bronco brands from subordination. Cooper protested and offered capability information the next day. Bronco selected L & L instead.

Viviano alleged losing the Bronco business forced a $1.65 million sale to Cooper and sued November 2. The difference from the intended price was unclear; $1.65 million was the sale price, not a damage award. It also alleged Bronco withheld previously ordered but undelivered wine after learning of the transfer.

sections.title: Michigan’s transfer statute supplies the standard
paragraphs: District Judge Cohn applied the Michigan wine-distribution provision barring withheld consent when the buyer met material and reasonable supplier qualifications. The statute required written notice, prohibited unreasonable delay, treated unapproved transfers as void, and measured reasonable standards against the supplier’s average criteria for new or renewed wholesalers over the preceding twenty-four months. Stable competition and the three-tier system informed that framework.

Bronco relied at the hearing on Gallo competition and Cooper’s spirits business. The court requested evidence on materiality, reasonableness, and compliance. At summary judgment it could not choose whose account was more convincing; the question was whether genuine disputes required a factfinder.

sections.title: Exceptions complicate the supplier’s asserted policies
sections.cue: The competing wine and spirits evidence
paragraphs: Scher identified twenty-eight Bronco distributors carrying Gallo and three more through contacts, denied prior knowledge of the policy, and noted L & L carried other premium competitors. Bronco did not deny the overlap. Franzia attributed it to acquired Napa Ridge relationships, later mergers, or markets lacking alternatives. All thirty-one were outside Michigan, only 7.5 percent of 413 distributors, and he identified two terminations after Gallo additions.

L & L itself did not carry Gallo, but ten of its nineteen out-state jobbers did. Its president emphasized no direct Bronco-jobber agreements and L & L’s ability to terminate for good cause or add distributors. That network helped Bronco select it, yet its known Gallo overlap left a factual question. The court did not treat criticisms from an unlisted, undeposed attorney and industry expert as the requested factual proof.

Scher also identified twenty-two Bronco distributors carrying spirits outside Michigan. He described Michigan’s state-controlled system, Cooper’s limited distribution-agent function, small spirits portfolio, and separate sales force. Franzia again distinguished inherited relationships and legal differences in other markets, stressing concentrated leverage among Michigan agents, including Cooper’s consortium. Those explanations did not conclusively establish either reasonableness or unreasonableness.

sections.title: A trial remains necessary
paragraphs: The court found disputes over national policies, exceptions, L & L’s selection, and Cooper’s satisfaction of material and reasonable standards. Neither exceptions alone nor Bronco’s percentage explanation established final liability or entitlement to judgment.

A cited commercial-code case involving a competitor-controlled buyer was factually and legally different, and a private beer-distribution arbitration did not control this wine statute. A prior supplier victory after a full bench trial illustrated that good faith, reasonable qualifications, cause, and notice could require factual resolution rather than dictate Bronco’s victory here.

The court found no need to decide Viviano’s complaint that the motion neglected undelivered orders. That claim was weakly pleaded and Bronco responded cursorily, without seriously seeking judgment on it. On December 11, 2001 the court denied Bronco’s motion, leaving the consent dispute for further proceedings and deciding neither a final damages figure nor the delivery claim’s legality.
